newsitem.title: USA: Quaker could sell Latin America pasta, fish units.
newsitem.headline: Quaker could sell Latin America pasta, fish units.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co, which has said it is considering the sale of some non-core operations, likely will sell its Latin America pasta and canned fish businesses, as well as its U.S. food service coffee operation, equity analysts said.
"Those are the businesses that stand out as being non-core," CS First Boston analyst Michael Mauboussin said.
Quaker officials declined to comment specifically on what operations the company would likely sell.
"We can't be more specific for disclosure reasons," Quaker spokesman Mark Dollins said.
Quaker reiterated Wednesday that it will continue to focus on grain-based products and on Gatorade sports drink, its largest single brand.
"That would point the finger at their food service coffee business," added Goldman Sachs anlayst Nomi Ghez, as well as the Latin American canned fish business.
She added that while Quaker's Latin American pasta business has been troubled from a profit standpoint, she expects the company to keep this operation.
Analysts stressed that whatever Quaker sells likely will be a comparatively small business. Over the past few years, Quaker has divested larger operations, such as its pet foods.

Mauboussin said he estimated Quaker's U.S. food service coffee business has about $100 million in annual sales. The Latin American pasta and canned fish operations, he estimated, have about $70 million in annual sales each.
In 1996, Quaker's total net sales were $5.2 billion.
Mauboussin added that another possible divestiture would be Quaker's European cereals business, which he estimated generates "a couple hundred million" in sales.
But other analysts said they expect Quaker to keep the European cereal operation.

Quaker's announcement that it may sell off some smaller businesses was part of a broader plan unveiled by the company, including the resumption of share repurchases which were suspended in the summer of 1994.
Quaker Chairman William Smithburg said Wednesday that about 3.5 million shares remain under a previous repurchase plan and additional buyback authority will be sought later.
BT Securities analyst John O'Neil said he expects the future share repurchases will be financed with proceeds from Snapple, which Quaker is selling after two years of losses.

"The share repurchases that the company is likely to make will be almost solely financed with Snapple proceeds because there will be little or no free cash flow from operations in 1997 and only about $35 million in 1998," O'Neil said.

The Quaker sale resulted in a $1.14 billion after-tax loss taken in the first quarter. Quaker has agreed to sell Snapple for $300 million and expects $250 million in cash proceeds from taxes paid previously, for a total value of $550 million.
Analysts also expressed little surprise that, as reported earlier, Smithburg plans to step down as chairman and chief executive officer soon after a successor is found.
Smithburg was criticized for buying Snapple about two years ago in a $1.8 billion deal.
"There has been a lot of buzz about it for some time," Mauboussin said. "Clearly with the Snapple situation, it makes a lot of sense."
